title: HTML and CSS for app developers
blurb: Semantics, forms, the box model, specificity, flexbox, grid and responsive layout: the CSS questions every frontend screen includes, and the layout bugs every CRUD screen hits.

questions.q: An app shell has a top bar, a side nav, the routed page and a footer. Which element should wrap the routed page?
choices: `<section>`
`<article>`
`<main>`
`<aside>`
questions.why: `<main>` marks the one primary-content region of the page, alongside `<header>`, `<nav>` and `<footer>`, and there should be only one visible at a time. `<section>` is a thematic group inside content and `<article>` is a self-contained item such as a post or card, so neither describes the page body itself.
questions.asked: A quick check that you structure a layout with landmarks rather than a stack of anonymous `div`s.

questions.q: Inside a `<section>` whose heading is `<h2>`, a card needs a title that looks small. Which element should the title use?
choices: `<h3>`, sized down with CSS, since the level reflects nesting
`<h6>`, since the heading level exists to set its visual size
`<h1>`, since each `<section>` restarts the heading outline
`<h2>`, since a card is a sibling of its section heading
questions.why: Heading levels describe the document outline, so a title nested under an `<h2>` is an `<h3>`, and CSS decides how big it looks. The "sections restart at `<h1>`" idea came from the HTML5 outline algorithm, which no browser implemented and the spec removed in 2022.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for the split between structure and styling; picking a level by font size is the junior tell.

questions.q: A table row has a Delete control that calls an API and does not change the URL. Which element fits best?
choices: `<a href="#">` with a click handler, so it is focusable and styled as a link
`<div onclick>` with a pointer cursor, styled to look like a button
`<a>` without an `href`, so it cannot navigate when it is clicked
`<button type="button">`, which is focusable and fires on Enter and Space
questions.why: Actions are buttons and navigation is links. A `<button>` gets focus, keyboard activation and disabled state for free. `href="#"` is a link that changes the URL hash and misleads, a `<div>` needs all of that behaviour rebuilt, and an `<a>` without `href` is not even focusable.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "and when is it a link?", so be ready to say: when it goes somewhere you could open in a new tab.

questions.q: You list orders with id, date, customer and total, and users sort by any column. Which markup fits?
choices: A CSS grid of `<div>`s, since a `<table>` can never be made responsive
A `<table>` with `<th>` headers in a `<thead>` and one `<tr>` per order
A `<ul>` of orders, each `<li>` holding the four values as `<span>`s
A `<dl>` with each order id as a `<dt>` and its fields as `<dd>`s
questions.why: Rows and columns of related values are tabular data, and `<table>` gives each cell a header relationship that tools and assistive tech rely on. Tables can be styled responsively (stacked rows, horizontal scroll), so dropping to `div`s loses the structure for no gain; lists and description lists do not model columns.
questions.asked: Checks that you did not absorb "tables are bad" from the table-layout era and apply it to actual data.

questions.q: What happens when the user clicks the words "Remember me"?
choices: Nothing, since a label needs a `for` attribute to be associated
The checkbox gets focus but stays unchecked until clicked directly
The checkbox toggles, since a wrapping label is associated with it
The text is selected, since label text is not an activation target
questions.why: A `<label>` is associated with the control either by `for`/`id` or by wrapping it, and clicking an associated label activates the control, so the checkbox toggles. That is why labelled checkboxes have a much bigger hit area than the tiny box itself.
questions.asked: A cheap question that exposes whether you have ever built a usable checkbox.

questions.q: This component renders once for each of three cart lines. What happens when a user clicks the label on the third line?
questions.code:
<!-- CartLine: rendered once per line -->
<label for="qty">Quantity</label>
<input id="qty" name="qty" type="number">
choices: The third line's input gets focus, since a label pairs with the nearest input
The first line's input gets focus, since `for` resolves to the first matching `id`
No input gets focus, since a duplicated `id` disables every label pointing at it
Every input with that `id` gets focus in turn, starting with the third
questions.why: `for` is resolved like `getElementById`, which returns the first element in document order, so every label focuses line one. Proximity plays no part. Fix it with unique ids per instance (React `useId`, or the line id in the attribute), or by wrapping the input inside the label so no id is needed.
questions.asked: This is a real bug in every component library that hard-codes ids, and naming `useId` or wrapping as the fix scores well.

questions.q: Which markup suits a phone number field, giving a phone keypad on mobile without number-input behaviour?
choices: `type="number"`, which shows a digit keypad and validates the digits
`type="text"` with `autocomplete="tel"`, which switches the keypad
`type="text"` with `maxlength="15"`, which mobile shows as digits
`type="tel"`, which shows a phone keypad and keeps the value as text
questions.why: `type="tel"` brings up the phone keypad but imposes no format, so "+44", spaces and leading zeros survive. `type="number"` is for quantities: it accepts `e` and decimals, sanitises "+44 20 7946 0000" to an empty value, and adds spinners and scroll-wheel changes. `autocomplete` helps autofill but does not choose the keyboard.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about mobile users filling in forms, and whether you know `type="number"` is not "any digits".

questions.q: The user clicks Sign up with the email field empty. What happens?
choices: The form submits, because `novalidate` skips the browser check on submit
The browser blocks the submit and shows its bubble, since `required` wins
The submit is blocked silently, with no message shown to the user at all
The form submits, and the browser strips the `required` attribute first
questions.why: `novalidate` turns off constraint validation at submit time only. The rules still exist: `input.validity`, `form.checkValidity()` and the `:invalid` pseudo-class keep working, which is exactly why teams use it: keep native rules, render their own messages. Nothing removes the attribute.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains the pattern: native attributes as the rule source, `novalidate` plus the validity API for custom error UI.

questions.q: What request body does this form submit?
questions.code:
<form method="post">
  <input id="email" value="a@b.co">
  <input name="code" value="X1" readonly>
  <fieldset disabled><input name="plan" value="pro"></fieldset>
  <input type="checkbox" name="terms">
  <input name="note" value="hi">
</form>
choices: `note=hi`
`code=X1&plan=pro&note=hi`
`code=X1&terms=&note=hi`
`code=X1&note=hi`
questions.why: Only named, enabled controls are submitted. The email input has no `name`, the input inside a disabled `<fieldset>` is disabled, and an unchecked checkbox sends nothing at all. `readonly` differs from `disabled`: the user cannot edit it, but its value is still submitted.
questions.asked: Explains a whole class of "the server never got the field" bugs; `readonly` versus `disabled` is the usual follow-up.

questions.q: With no other CSS applied, how much horizontal space does `.card` take up, excluding margin?
choices: 300px
344px
340px
322px
questions.why: The default `box-sizing: content-box` applies `width` to the content only, so padding and border are added: 300 + 2×20 + 2×2 = 344. With `box-sizing: border-box` the card would be 300px with a 256px content area, which is why most resets set it globally.
questions.asked: Checks that you know why the universal `border-box` reset exists, not just that you paste it.

questions.q: The 24px gap appears above the grey card, outside its background, instead of inside it. Why?
questions.code:
.card { background: #eee; }  /* no padding, no border */
.card h2 { margin-top: 24px; } /* first child */
choices: Headings are inline by default, so their vertical margins push outward
The card has `height: auto`, which moves child margins outside its box
A first child's `margin-top` is always applied to its parent instead
The heading's top margin collapses through the card, since nothing separates them
questions.why: Vertical margins of a block parent and its first child collapse when no padding, border or new formatting context separates them, so the margin ends up outside the card. It does not happen in every case: padding, a border, `display: flow-root`, or a flex or grid parent all stop it.
questions.asked: A classic layout bug; strong candidates name the collapse and give a fix such as padding or `flow-root`.

questions.q: You set `width: 120px` and `margin-top: 12px` on a `<span>`, and neither has a visible effect. Why?
choices: A span is inline: `width` is ignored and vertical margins do not move lines
A span only accepts sizes in `em`, so a `px` width is silently dropped
`width` needs a `height` set too, and the margin needs `position: relative`
Browser defaults reset margins on inline text elements to zero pixels
questions.why: Inline boxes flow as text: `width` and `height` do not apply, and vertical margins do not affect line layout. `display: inline-block` keeps it in the line while honouring width and margins; `display: block` puts it on its own line.
questions.asked: Checks that you know inline, block and inline-block as layout modes rather than trial and error.

questions.q: What is the computed `padding-top` of `.media`, a child of `.box`?
choices: 50px, half the height of the containing block
0px, because `.media` itself has no height set
200px, half the width of the containing block
Half the viewport height, the same as `50vh`
questions.why: Percentage padding and margin resolve against the containing block's width, even on the top and bottom, so this is 50% of 400px. That quirk powered the old "padding-top: 56.25%" 16:9 trick, which `aspect-ratio` now replaces.
questions.asked: An edge case that tells the interviewer you have met legacy responsive-embed code and know the modern replacement.

questions.q: The link is `<a class="link active">` inside `<nav id="main" class="nav">`. What colour is it?
choices: Red: three classes add up to more than one id
Blue: one id outweighs any number of classes
Red: equal weight, so the later rule wins
Red: the selector with more parts always wins
questions.why: Specificity compares ids, then classes, then elements as separate columns: `#main a` is (1,0,1) and `.nav .link.active` is (0,3,0), so the id column decides and no number of classes carries over. Source order only breaks exact ties.
questions.asked: The foundation for every "why is my style not applying" question that follows.

questions.q: A vendor stylesheet sets `.btn { color: white !important; }`. Which change in your own stylesheet makes your button text black?
choices: `#app #app .btn { color: black; }`, a normal rule with far higher specificity
An inline `style="color: black"` attribute on the button element itself
`#app .btn { color: black !important; }`, an important rule with more specificity
Loading your stylesheet after the vendor one so your normal rule is later
questions.why: Important declarations form their own tier above all normal ones, including inline styles, so only another `!important` can beat it; within that tier specificity and order apply again. That escalation is why `!important` in shared CSS is a smell, and why `@layer` is the cleaner tool for taming vendor styles.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that `!important` is a separate tier, and ideally a better alternative than piling on more of it.

questions.q: A `.title` sits inside `.card` inside `#app`. What colour is it, and what happens if `:where` becomes `:is`?
choices: Red; with `:is(#app)` it would stay red
Blue; with `:is(#app)` it would stay blue
Red; with `:is(#app)` it would become blue
Blue; with `:is(#app)` it would become red
questions.why: `:where()` always adds zero specificity, so the second rule is (0,1,0) and loses to (0,2,0) despite coming later. `:is()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument, so `:is(#app) .title` becomes (1,1,0) and wins. That is why libraries wrap their defaults in `:where()`: they stay easy to override.
questions.asked: Shows you know the modern selectors and why design systems ship zero-specificity defaults.

questions.q: What colour is a `.btn` inside `#app`?
choices: Green: unlayered styles beat every layer for normal rules
Red: `#app .btn` has the highest specificity of the three
Blue: `components` comes last in the declared layer order
Red: `base` is declared first, so it takes the priority
questions.why: Layer order is checked before specificity. For normal declarations, later layers beat earlier ones and unlayered styles beat all layers, so green wins and `#app .btn` loses despite its id. Blue would win if the last rule were removed. Important declarations reverse the layer order.
questions.asked: Cascade layers are the modern answer to specificity wars, and knowing unlayered styles win is the detail that trips people up.

questions.q: The close button lands in the top-right corner of the page, not of the card. Which change fixes it?
questions.code:
.card  { padding: 16px; }  /* the button's parent */
.close { position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px; }
choices: Change `.close` to `position: relative`
Add `position: relative` to `.card`
Add `overflow: hidden` to `.card`
Add `display: block` to `.card`
questions.why: An absolutely positioned element is placed against its nearest positioned ancestor; with none, it uses the initial containing block, which is the page. `position: relative` on the card makes it that ancestor without moving it. Making the button relative would offset it from its normal spot instead.
questions.asked: The most common positioning bug, and the explanation of containing blocks is what separates understanding from habit.

questions.q: A `position: sticky; top: 0` list header scrolls away with the content instead of sticking. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The header has no `z-index`, so sticky positioning never activates
Its parent lacks `position: relative`, which sticky uses as an anchor
An ancestor between it and the page scroller has `overflow: hidden`
Sticky only works on block `div`s, not on `thead` or `th` elements
questions.why: Sticky sticks within its nearest scrolling ancestor, and any `overflow` other than `visible` creates one; if that element does not itself scroll, the header never sticks. It also stays inside its parent, so a parent no taller than the header gives it no room. `z-index` only affects painting, and sticky table headers work in current browsers.
questions.asked: A daily CRUD-table bug; naming the overflow ancestor quickly signals real debugging experience.

questions.q: A `position: fixed` overlay is confined to a card's box instead of covering the viewport. Which property on the card causes this?
choices: `position: relative`
`overflow: hidden`
`display: flex`
`transform: scale(1)`
questions.why: `transform` (also `filter`, `perspective`, `contain: paint` and `will-change: transform`) makes an element the containing block for fixed descendants, so "fixed" becomes relative to the card. `position: relative` and `overflow: hidden` only affect absolute children. The usual fix is to render the modal in a portal at the end of `body`.
questions.asked: This bug shows up when a modal lives inside an animated card, and it explains why modal libraries use portals.

questions.q: The open menu renders behind `.content` despite `z-index: 9999`. Why?
choices: `.menu` stacks inside `.header`'s context, which sits below `.content`'s 2
Browsers clamp `z-index` values above 999, so 9999 is treated as 999
An absolute element ignores `z-index` unless its parent is `static`
`.content` comes later in the DOM, and that beats any `z-index` on `.menu`
questions.why: `.header` with a position and a `z-index` creates a stacking context, so everything inside it, menu included, is painted as one layer at level 1. That layer sits below `.content` at level 2, whatever the child values. Fix it by raising `.header` above `.content`, or by rendering the menu outside the header.
questions.asked: The "z-index 9999 does not work" bug; interviewers want the words stacking context and a fix that does not escalate the number.

questions.q: In a container with `flex-direction: column` and a fixed height, what does `justify-content: center` do?
choices: Centres the items horizontally, since justify always means horizontal
Centres the items vertically, as the main axis now runs top to bottom
Nothing, since `justify-content` only applies to row flex containers
Centres the text inside each item rather than the items themselves
questions.why: `justify-content` works along the main axis and `align-items` along the cross axis, and `flex-direction` decides which is which. In a column the main axis is vertical, so the roles swap compared with a row.
questions.asked: Checks for the axis model rather than memorised "justify is horizontal", which breaks the first time a column is used.

questions.q: What does the shorthand `flex: 1` expand to?
choices: `flex: 1 1 auto`, so items share leftover space after their content
`flex: 1 0 auto`, so items grow to fill space but never shrink
`flex: 1 1 0%`, so items split space equally regardless of content
`flex: 1 0 0%`, so items grow equally but can never shrink
questions.why: A single number sets `flex-grow` and implies `flex-shrink: 1` and `flex-basis: 0%`, so columns with `flex: 1` come out equal whatever their content. `flex: auto` is the `1 1 auto` version, where longer content ends up with a wider column.
questions.asked: Explains the "why are my equal columns not equal" question, which is the likely follow-up.

questions.q: Long titles push the row wider than its container instead of truncating with an ellipsis. Which change fixes it?
choices: Add `min-width: 0` to `.title`
Add `flex-shrink: 1` to `.main`
Add `width: 100%` to `.title`
Add `min-width: 0` to `.main`
questions.why: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which stops them shrinking below their content's minimum width, and nowrap text makes that the full title. `min-width: 0` on the flex item lets it shrink so the child can clip. `.title` is not a flex item, and `flex: 1` already sets shrink to 1.
questions.asked: Probably the most common flexbox bug in real apps; knowing `min-width: auto` is the cause is a strong experience signal.

questions.q: Why is `gap` usually better than margins on flex items for spacing them?
choices: It adds space only between items, so no stray space at ends or wrapped rows
It is faster, because margins on flex items make the browser recalculate layout
It adds equal space around every item, including the container's edges
It spaces grid tracks only; in flexbox it just sets the default margin
questions.why: `gap` puts space between adjacent items and between wrapped lines, never on the outer edges, so there is no `:last-child { margin: 0 }` or negative-margin wrapper. Flexbox `gap` has been supported in every evergreen browser since 2021, and it has no performance edge over margins.
questions.asked: Shows whether your CSS knowledge is current; the negative-margin wrapper is the pre-2021 answer.

questions.q: How wide is each column, with no gap?
choices: 200px, 267px and 533px
160px, 213px and 427px
200px, 200px and 400px
200px, 300px and 300px
questions.why: `fr` shares out the space left after fixed tracks: 800 − 200 = 600, split 1:2 into 200 and 400. It is not a fraction of the whole container, which is where 267/533 comes from.
questions.asked: A quick check that you can predict a grid layout on paper before opening DevTools.

questions.q: The grid holds only two cards. How wide is each, and what changes with `auto-fill`?
choices: 200px each; with `auto-fill` they stretch to 500px each
500px each; with `auto-fill` they stay 200px beside empty tracks
200px each in both cases, since five tracks always fit
500px each in both cases, since `1fr` absorbs free space
questions.why: Both create as many 200px-minimum tracks as fit (five). `auto-fit` then collapses the empty ones, so the two cards share the full 1000px; `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks, so each card stays one fifth wide. Pick `auto-fill` when a lone card should not stretch across the page.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "which one for a product grid", and the answer depends on whether a lone card should stretch.

questions.q: Which layout job is grid a clearly better fit for than flexbox?
choices: A form whose labels and inputs line up in columns across every row
A toolbar of buttons whose widths depend on the length of their text
A single row of items that pushes the last one to the far right edge
A tag list that wraps chips of different widths onto following lines
questions.why: Grid is two-dimensional: tracks align across rows and columns at once, which a form of label/input pairs needs. Flexbox is one-dimensional and content-sized, so toolbars, `margin-left: auto` pushes and wrapping chip lists are its natural jobs; grid would force chips into equal columns.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a rule of thumb (one axis versus two, content-sized versus track-sized), not "I use grid for everything".

questions.q: A page has media queries for narrow screens but no viewport meta tag. What does a phone browser do with it?
choices: Uses the phone's real width anyway, since the tag only controls zooming
Ignores every media query until the tag is added to the document head
Uses the real width but scales all body text up to at least 16px
Lays it out about 980px wide and zooms out, so narrow queries never match
questions.why: Without `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`, mobile browsers assume a desktop page, lay it out on a virtual viewport of about 980px and shrink it to fit, so `max-width: 600px` queries never fire. Media queries still run, just against the wrong width.
questions.asked: The first thing to check when "the mobile styles do not work", so it is a common screening question.

questions.q: On a 1400px-wide screen, how many columns does `.grid` have?
choices: Three: the larger `min-width` query takes priority
Two: both queries match, and the later rule wins
One: base rules outside a query always win
It varies by browser, as overlapping queries are undefined
questions.why: Media queries add no specificity. At 1400px both match, the selectors tie, and source order decides, so the 768px rule wins. Mobile-first CSS works only when `min-width` queries go in ascending order, each overriding the one before.
questions.asked: A real ordering bug; the strong answer states the ascending `min-width` convention.

questions.q: What padding does the paragraph get?
choices: 32px on all four sides of the paragraph
40px on all four sides of the paragraph
40px top and bottom, 32px left and right
32px top and bottom, 40px left and right
questions.why: `em` is relative to the element's own font size, which the paragraph inherits as 20px, so 2em is 40px. `rem` is relative to the root font size, 16px, so 2rem is 32px. Use `rem` for consistent spacing and type scales, and `em` when a value should scale with its component's text.
questions.asked: Tests the unit choice behind accessible, zoom-friendly layouts, and the reason nested `em` values compound.

questions.q: On a 1440px-wide laptop with a device pixel ratio of 2 and an empty cache, which file will the browser most likely fetch?
choices: `card-400.jpg`: the `sizes` value names a 400px slot, which it matches
`card-1600.jpg`: the widest candidate is used above the 1024px breakpoint
`card-1600.jpg`: the 1440px viewport needs the next size up from 800
`card-800.jpg`: the slot is 400px and each CSS pixel needs 2 image pixels
questions.why: `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will display (400px here, since the query matches), and it multiplies by the pixel ratio to get 800 needed pixels, then picks the closest `w` candidate. Without `sizes` it would assume `100vw` and fetch the 1600px file for a 400px slot.
questions.asked: Responsive images are a common gap; explaining `sizes` as the missing half of `srcset` stands out.

questions.q: The root font size is 16px and the viewport is 600px wide. What font size does the heading get?
choices: 24px, since the preferred value is below the minimum and the minimum wins
48px, since the maximum is the fallback whenever the preferred value is out of range
12.5px, since 2vw + 0.5rem is 12px plus half a pixel
20px, since the preferred value 2vw + 0.5rem resolves to 12px plus 8px
questions.why: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` resolves the preferred value first: 2vw at 600px is 12px, plus 0.5rem (8px) gives 20px, which is under the 1.5rem (24px) minimum, so the minimum wins. The heading only starts growing once the viewport passes 800px and stops at 3rem. Nothing about it is 12.5px, because `0.5rem` is 8px, not half a pixel; and the max is a ceiling, not a fallback. A rem term in the preferred value also keeps fluid type scaling when the user zooms text.
questions.asked: Fluid typography with `clamp()` replaced a stack of media queries; interviewers want you to evaluate one on paper, including the rem term that keeps it zoomable.

questions.q: You set `font-family` on `body`, yet every `<button>` and `<input>` still renders in the system font. Why?
choices: Buttons are replaced elements, which never take any text styles
The UA stylesheet gives form controls their own `font` value
`font-family` only inherits into block-level descendants
Form controls read fonts from the OS theme, not from CSS
questions.why: Browsers' default stylesheets set a `font` on form controls, and a directly set value always beats an inherited one, so the body font never reaches them. Resets add `button, input, select, textarea { font: inherit; }`; controls are fully stylable, they just do not inherit by default.
questions.asked: Every CSS reset has this line; interviewers ask it to see whether you understand inherited versus directly set values.

questions.q: `.card` has `color: navy` and `border: 1px solid grey`. Which of these do the paragraphs inside the card pick up?
choices: Both: children inherit every property set on a parent
Neither: only properties set on `:root` are inherited
The border only, because box properties cascade down
The colour only: `color` inherits, `border` does not
questions.why: Each property is defined as inherited or not: text properties like `color`, `font` and `line-height` inherit, while box properties like `border`, `padding` and `margin` do not. Otherwise every nested element would draw its own border.
questions.asked: Knowing which properties inherit is the basis for writing less CSS and for debugging styles that seem to leak.

questions.q:
A `

` sits inside `.card { color: navy; }`. What colour does it get with this rule?
choices: The spec's initial value (usually black), not navy
Navy, because `initial` takes the parent's value
Whatever the UA stylesheet sets for paragraphs
Navy: `initial` is ignored on inherited properties
questions.why: `initial` means the property's initial value from the spec (`canvastext`, black in a light scheme), ignoring both the parent and the browser stylesheet. `inherit` would give navy, and `revert` would roll back to the UA stylesheet's value.
questions.asked: The four global keywords (`inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`) are a favourite way to probe cascade knowledge past specificity.

questions.q: A design system resets its buttons with `all: unset`. What happens to the button's `display` and `color`?
choices: `display` becomes `inline`; `color` inherits from the parent
`display` goes back to `inline-block`; `color` turns black
Each goes back to the browser's default button style
Each inherits the parent element's computed value
questions.why: `unset` acts as `inherit` for inherited properties such as `color` and as `initial` for the rest, and the initial value of `display` is `inline`. Going back to the browser's button look is what `all: revert` does.
questions.asked: It explains why an `all: unset` button suddenly sits inline and loses its focus ring, which you then have to restore deliberately.

questions.q: The menu has nested sub-lists. Which `<li>` elements does this selector match?
choices: Every `<li>` anywhere inside `.menu`, at any depth
Only the first `<li>` inside `.menu`
Only `<li>` elements that are direct children of `.menu`
Every `<li>` that comes after `.menu` anywhere in the document
questions.why: `>` is the child combinator, so only the top-level items match; the space in `.menu li` is the descendant combinator, which would also reach the sub-list items. Following siblings are what `~` targets.
questions.asked: A basic combinator check that comes up whenever nested menus or comment threads pick up styles they should not.

questions.q:
An article has an `

` followed by three `

` elements. Which paragraphs does `h2 + p` match?
choices: All three paragraphs that follow the heading
None, because `+` only matches parent and child
Only the last paragraph before the next heading
Only the paragraph straight after the heading
questions.why: `+` is the next-sibling combinator: it matches a `p` that immediately follows an `h2` with the same parent. The subsequent-sibling combinator `h2 ~ p` would match all three.
questions.asked: Used for "intro paragraph" styling; the follow-up is usually how `~` differs.

questions.q:
Each form row is `
`. Which selector styles the whole row red when its input is invalid?
choices: `.field input:invalid`
`.field:parent(input:invalid)`
`input:invalid ~ .field`
`.field:has(input:invalid)`
questions.why: `:has()` matches an element based on its descendants, so it is the "parent selector" CSS lacked for years and is supported in all current browsers. `.field input:invalid` styles only the input, `<` is not a CSS combinator, and `~` looks at later siblings, not ancestors.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask about `:has()` to see whether your CSS knowledge is current; a strong answer mentions it replaces JavaScript that toggled parent classes.

questions.q:
What colour is `

`, given this CSS?
choices: Blue: `.note` comes later and `:not()` adds no weight
Red: `:not(#intro)` counts as an id, so it outweighs a class
Blue: a class selector always beats an element selector
Red: negation pseudo-classes add one to the class-selector column
questions.why: `:not()`, `:is()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their most specific argument, so `p:not(#intro)` is (1,0,1) and beats `.note` at (0,1,0) even though no id is actually matched. Only `:where()` contributes zero.
questions.asked: A classic "why does this innocent-looking rule win" puzzle; strong candidates know which functional pseudo-classes carry weight.

questions.q: What colour is the `.btn` inside `#app`?
choices: Red: its selector has an id, so it has more specificity
Red: layered rules are applied after unlayered ones
Blue: unlayered styles beat every normal layered rule
Blue: specificity is ignored and later source order wins
questions.why: Cascade layers are compared before specificity, and normal declarations outside any layer sit in an implicit final layer that beats all named layers. Specificity only matters between rules in the same layer; source order is not what decides here.
questions.asked: Cascade layers are the modern answer to specificity wars, and interviewers check you know layer order trumps selector weight.

questions.q: What colour is the `.btn`?
choices: Blue: `components` is declared after `base` in the order
Red: the `base` block appears last in the source, so it wins
Red: its selector has an id, and ids always win
Blue: the first `@layer` block in the file wins
questions.why: Layer order is fixed by the first time each name appears, here the `@layer base, components;` statement, and later layers win for normal declarations. Where the blocks sit afterwards and how specific their selectors are does not change that.
questions.asked: Declaring the order up front is the idiom teams use; interviewers want you to explain why it makes stylesheet load order irrelevant.

questions.q: Both rules are `!important`. What colour is the `.btn`?
choices: Blue: `theme` is the later layer, so it wins
Blue: with equal specificity, the last rule wins
Red: important declarations reverse the layer order
Neither: two important rules cancel out, so it inherits
questions.why: For `!important` declarations the layer order flips, so the earliest layer wins; that lets a base or reset layer lock something down that later layers cannot override. For normal declarations `theme` would win.
questions.asked: A deep cascade question; knowing the inversion shows you understand why `!important` exists at all, not just that it is "bad".

questions.q: A vendor date-picker stylesheet keeps beating your overrides with long selectors. How do you make all of its rules lose to your unlayered CSS?
choices: Link it after your own stylesheet so its rules come later
Add `!important` to every rule you want to override
Import it into a layer: `@import url(vendor.css) layer(vendor);`
Put your own rules in `@layer app` and leave the vendor CSS alone
questions.why: Anything in a layer loses to unlayered normal styles, whatever its specificity, so importing the vendor file into a layer disarms it without editing it. Putting your own CSS in a layer does the opposite and makes the unlayered vendor rules win.
questions.asked: A practical question about taming third-party CSS; it tells the interviewer you can apply layers, not just recite them.

questions.q: Two stacked blocks: the first has `margin-bottom: 20px` and the second `margin-top: 30px`. In normal block flow, how far apart are they?
choices: 30px, because the vertical margins collapse
50px, because the two margins add together
20px, because the first margin takes priority
25px, because collapsing averages the margins
questions.why: Adjacent vertical margins in block flow collapse into one margin the size of the larger. Horizontal margins never collapse, and the effect disappears inside flex and grid containers.
questions.asked: Margin collapsing is behind many "my spacing is wrong" bugs and is a staple junior CSS question.

questions.q: The same two blocks (`margin-bottom: 20px`, then `margin-top: 30px`) are now children of a `display: flex; flex-direction: column` container. How far apart are they?
choices: 30px, the same as in normal block flow
20px, the margin of the first child only
0px, because flex items ignore vertical margins
50px, as flex item margins do not collapse
questions.why: Margin collapsing is a block-flow behaviour; flex and grid items keep both margins, so they add up. That difference is one reason teams switch stacks to `gap`, which behaves the same everywhere.
questions.asked: Checks that you know collapsing is specific to block layout, which explains spacing that changes when someone adds `display: flex`.

questions.q: A wrapper contains only floated images and collapses to zero height, so its background vanishes. What is the modern one-line fix on the wrapper?
choices: `display: flow-root`
`clear: both`
`height: auto`
`position: relative`
questions.why: `display: flow-root` makes the wrapper a new block formatting context, which contains its floats so its height includes them. `clear` belongs on an element after the floats, `height: auto` is already the default, and positioning does not change float containment.
questions.asked: Floats are rare in new code but common in legacy and email CSS; this tells the interviewer you know the clean fix rather than the clearfix hack.

questions.q: Adding `border: 2px solid` on `:hover` makes neighbouring menu items jump. Why does `outline: 2px solid` not cause the jump?
choices: Outlines are drawn outside the box and take up no layout space
Outlines are always drawn inside the padding box
Browsers only redraw outlines on the next animation frame, after layout
Outlines ignore `box-sizing` and only apply on focus
questions.why: A border is part of the box model, so adding one grows the element (unless it already had a transparent border) and pushes its neighbours. An outline is painted over the layout without affecting it, which is also why focus rings use it.
questions.asked: A simple layout-shift question; a strong answer also mentions the transparent-border trick or `box-shadow` alternatives.

questions.q: Text sits in the inner `.a` element. What is its computed font size?
choices: 24px, because `em` is relative to the root size
16px, because `em` is ignored when nested
32px, because each level adds 8px to the size
36px, because `em` compounds on the parent size
questions.why: For `font-size`, `em` is relative to the parent's computed font size, so the outer div is 24px and the inner one 1.5 × 24 = 36px. `rem` avoids the compounding by always using the root size.
questions.asked: The rem-versus-em question; a good answer says when `em` compounding is useful, such as padding that scales with a component's own text.

questions.q: A full-screen mobile checkout uses `height: 100vh`, and its bottom Pay button hides behind the browser's address bar. Which value fixes it?
choices: `100lvh`, the viewport height with the toolbar retracted
`100%` on the checkout, which always equals the visible area
`100dvh`, which tracks the viewport as the toolbar moves
`100vmax`, the larger of the viewport width and height
questions.why: On mobile, `vh` is the large viewport (toolbars hidden), so content overflows when they are showing. `dvh` follows the current visible height; `svh` is the smallest viewport if you prefer no resizing. `lvh` is exactly the size that caused the bug.
questions.asked: A real mobile bug; knowing `svh`, `lvh` and `dvh` shows your CSS knowledge is current and that you test on phones.

questions.q: What does `max-width: 65ch` on an article's text column do?
choices: Caps each line at exactly 65 characters of any width
Caps the column at 65% of its container's width
Caps the column at 65 times the element's font size
Caps it at 65 widths of the "0" glyph in its font
questions.why: One `ch` is the advance width of the "0" character in the element's font, so 65ch gives roughly 60–75 characters per line in proportional fonts, a comfortable measure. It is not an exact character count, and `em` is the unit tied to font size.
questions.asked: A quick unit check that also lets you talk about readable line length in content-heavy pages.

questions.q: A sidebar's child has `height: 50%`, but it stays as tall as its content. The sidebar itself has no height set. Why?
choices: Percentage heights only work on absolutely positioned elements
The sidebar's height is `auto`, so the percentage becomes `auto`
Percentage heights resolve against the viewport height, not the parent
Percentages need `box-sizing: border-box` on the child to apply
questions.why: A percentage height needs a containing block with a definite height; when the parent is sized by its content, the child's percentage behaves as `auto`. Stretch the parent (flex or grid) or give it a definite height instead.
questions.asked: A daily frustration; interviewers like hearing that percentage widths and heights resolve differently and why.

questions.q: Which of these leaves the element invisible but still clickable?
choices: `display: none`
`visibility: hidden`
`opacity: 0`
`content-visibility: hidden`
questions.why: `opacity: 0` only changes painting, so the element keeps its space and still receives clicks and focus. `visibility: hidden` keeps the space but ignores pointer events, and `display: none` removes the box entirely.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "and which of them hides content from screen readers", so know all three.

questions.q: A toolbar is `<div class="toolbar" hidden>` and the stylesheet has `.toolbar { display: flex; }`. What does the user see?
choices: The toolbar: author CSS overrides the UA's `display: none`
Nothing: the `hidden` attribute always wins over CSS
Nothing until JavaScript removes the attribute
The toolbar, but with `visibility: hidden` applied by the UA
questions.why: `hidden` works only through a UA stylesheet rule `[hidden] { display: none }`, which any author `display` value beats. Resets often add `[hidden] { display: none !important; }` so the attribute keeps working.
questions.asked: A real bug that ships often; the answer shows you know how HTML attributes and CSS interact through the UA stylesheet.

questions.q: A form's fields are wrapped in `<div class="row">` elements, and you want each field to be a direct grid item of the form. What does `.row { display: contents; }` do?
choices: Makes `.row` a subgrid that shares the form's tracks
Hides `.row` but keeps it available to screen readers
Makes `.row` fill its grid cell with its own contents
Removes `.row`'s box so its children become grid items
questions.why: With `display: contents` the element generates no box of its own and its children are laid out as if they were children of its parent, so they join the form's grid. That is different from `subgrid`, which keeps the wrapper as a grid item that reuses its parent's tracks.
questions.asked: It shows you can fix a layout without changing markup that a component library or framework controls.

questions.q:
An `` inside a bordered `
` leaves a few pixels of empty space under it. What causes the gap?
choices: The image is inline and sits on the text baseline
The browser adds default `margin-bottom` to images
The div's `line-height` is applied as extra padding
The image's intrinsic size includes a transparent row
questions.why: Images are inline by default, so they sit on the baseline and leave room below it for descenders. `display: block` on the image (or `vertical-align: middle`) removes the gap, which is why resets set `img { display: block; }`.
questions.asked: A small bug that tests whether you understand inline formatting rather than reaching for negative margins.

questions.q: A block element has `width: 600px`. Which declaration centres it horizontally inside its wider parent?
choices: `text-align: center` on the element
`vertical-align: middle` on the element
`align-self: center` on the element
`margin-inline: auto` on the element
questions.why: Auto inline margins split the free space equally, centring a block with a known width. `text-align` centres inline content inside a block, `align-self` needs a flex or grid parent, and `vertical-align` applies to inline and table cells.
questions.asked: The oldest CSS interview question; a strong answer adds how you would do it with flex or grid, too.

questions.q: This rule shows no ellipsis; long titles wrap onto a second line instead. What is missing?
choices: `display: inline-block`, as ellipsis needs an inline box
`white-space: nowrap`, so the text overflows sideways
`width: 100%`, so the box has an explicit width
`overflow-wrap: anywhere`, so words can be truncated
questions.why: `text-overflow` only applies when inline content overflows the box horizontally, and text that is allowed to wrap never does. The single-line ellipsis needs all three: `overflow: hidden`, `white-space: nowrap` and `text-overflow: ellipsis`.
questions.asked: It is on every table and card; interviewers use it to see if you know why the three properties go together.

questions.q: Long URLs in user comments overflow their card. Which declaration wraps them only when a word would not fit otherwise?
choices: `word-break: break-all`, which only breaks overflowing words
`white-space: pre-wrap`, which wraps long unbroken strings
`hyphens: auto`, which splits any string at a hyphen
`overflow-wrap: anywhere`, which breaks only if it must
questions.why: `overflow-wrap: anywhere` (or `break-word`) allows breaks inside a word only when there is no other way to fit the line, leaving normal text alone. `word-break: break-all` breaks every word at the edge, and `hyphens` only works on dictionary words in a declared language.
questions.asked: User-generated content always contains a 200-character URL; this shows you have dealt with it properly.

questions.q: A dropdown inside a card must not escape its z-index into the rest of the page. Which declaration on the card creates a stacking context without other side effects?
choices: `isolation: isolate`
`position: relative`
`overflow: hidden`
`display: flow-root`
questions.why: `isolation: isolate` exists to create a stacking context and does nothing else. `position: relative` alone does not create one without a `z-index`, `overflow: hidden` would clip the dropdown, and `flow-root` creates a block formatting context, not a stacking context.
questions.asked: z-index questions are standard; naming `isolation` shows you manage stacking contexts on purpose rather than escalating numbers.

questions.q: Inside a `position: relative` card, where does this box end up?
choices: At the top-left, since auto margins are 0 when positioned
Stretched to fill the card, ignoring its width and height
Centred horizontally only; vertical auto margins are 0
Centred both ways inside the card's padding box
questions.why: With all four insets set and a fixed size, the leftover space in each direction is shared by the auto margins, which centres the box both ways. Without the explicit width and height, `inset: 0` would stretch it instead.
questions.asked: It shows you understand how absolute positioning resolves auto margins, the mechanism behind a classic centring technique.

questions.q: An icon button's inline SVG should always match the button text's colour, including on hover and in dark mode. What should the SVG use?
choices: `fill: inherit`, which copies the parent's `fill`
`fill: auto`, which lets the browser pick a contrast
`fill: var(--text)`, which resolves on `:root` only
`fill: currentColor`, the element's own `color` value
questions.why: `currentColor` resolves to the element's computed `color`, which the SVG inherits from the button, so every colour change on the button reaches the icon. `inherit` would copy the parent's `fill`, which is not the text colour, and `fill: auto` does not exist.
questions.asked: A small detail that shows you build icon systems that theme cleanly without per-state overrides.

questions.q: With native CSS nesting, which elements does the nested rule select?
choices: A `.sidebar` element inside a `.card`
A `.card` element inside a `.sidebar`
An element with both `.card` and `.sidebar`
Nothing, since `&` must start the selector
questions.why: `&` stands for the parent rule's selector wherever it appears, so `.sidebar &` means `.sidebar .card`. `&` may appear anywhere in the nested selector; it is a Sass habit that it has to come first.
questions.asked: Native nesting shipped in all engines; interviewers ask about `&` placement to see whether you know it beyond Sass.

questions.q: Inside `.tab { … }` using native CSS nesting, what is the difference between `&.active` and `& .active`?
choices: The first matches `.tab.active`; the second matches an `.active` inside `.tab`
None: whitespace around `&` is ignored when nesting
The first matches an `.active` inside `.tab`; the second matches `.tab.active`
The first is invalid without `:is()`; the second matches `.tab .active`
questions.why: Without a space `&` joins the class to the parent selector (same element); the space is the descendant combinator. Mixing them up silently styles the wrong element, which is a common nesting bug.
questions.asked: A small syntax point that catches real bugs in code review.

questions.q: Your app will ship an Arabic version with `dir="rtl"`. Why write `padding-inline-start: 1rem` instead of `padding-left: 1rem`?
choices: It applies padding on both inline sides at once
It is shorthand that sets the top and left padding
It maps to the left in LTR and the right in RTL
It only applies when the text direction is RTL
questions.why: Logical properties follow the writing direction: `inline-start` is the side where text begins, so layouts mirror correctly for right-to-left languages without a second stylesheet. `padding-inline` is the one that sets both sides.
questions.asked: Increasingly asked by product teams with international users; it shows you write CSS that survives localisation.

questions.q: In a flex container with the default `flex-direction: row`, which property centres the items vertically?
choices: `justify-content: center`
`align-content: center`
`vertical-align: middle`
`align-items: center`
questions.why: In a row the main axis is horizontal, so `justify-content` works left to right and `align-items` works on the cross axis, top to bottom. `vertical-align` does nothing to flex items, and `align-content` spaces wrapped lines rather than items in a single line.
questions.asked: The main-axis versus cross-axis distinction is the core flexbox concept; everything else builds on it.

questions.q: Three cards in a flex row have different amounts of text, yet all three render the same height. Why?
choices: Flex items get the height of the tallest item by rule
The default `align-items: stretch` fills the line's height
`flex: 1` on each card equalises their heights
Flex containers set `height: 100%` on all of their children
questions.why: The initial value of `align-items` is `stretch`, so items without a fixed cross size stretch to fill the line, which is as tall as the tallest item. Set `align-items: flex-start` to let each card keep its content height; `flex` only affects the main axis.
questions.asked: It explains both the "equal-height cards for free" win and the "why is my button stretched" bug.

questions.q: The container is 600px wide with no gap. How wide do `.a` and `.b` end up?
choices: About 233px and 367px: the 400px left over is split 1 : 2
200px and 400px, split 1 : 2 across the whole row
300px each, because the bases are equal
100px and 500px, as `.b` takes all the free space
questions.why: Flex-grow divides the free space left after the bases, not the whole container: 600 − 200 = 400px, shared 1 : 2, gives 133⅓px and 266⅔px on top of each 100px basis. A 1 : 2 split of the full width only happens when the bases are 0, as with `flex: 1` and `flex: 2`.
questions.asked: Working the numbers shows you understand the flex algorithm rather than treating grow values as percentages.

questions.q: Three tabs have labels of very different lengths, and they should be exactly equal widths across the bar. Which declaration on each tab does that?
choices: `flex: auto`
`flex: initial`
`flex: none`
`flex: 1`
questions.why: `flex: 1` sets a basis of 0, so all the space is free space and is shared equally, whatever the content. `flex: auto` starts from each tab's content width and then adds equal shares, so longer labels stay wider; `none` and `initial` do not grow at all.
questions.asked: Choosing between `flex: 1` and `flex: auto` is a real decision on every toolbar; interviewers like the "basis 0 versus basis auto" explanation.

questions.q: A navbar is a flex row of links followed by a Log out button. What is the simplest way to push only the button to the far right?
choices: `float: right` on the button
`justify-content: space-between` on the nav
`align-self: flex-end` on the button
`margin-left: auto` on the button
questions.why: An auto margin on a flex item absorbs all the free space on that side, pushing the button and anything after it to the end. `space-between` would also spread the links apart, `float` is ignored on flex items, and `align-self` works on the cross axis.
questions.asked: The auto-margin trick is a sign of someone who has built real navbars with flexbox.

questions.q: A sidebar has `width: 280px` in a flex row. When the main area holds a wide table, the sidebar gets narrower than 280px. What stops that?
choices: `flex-shrink: 0` on the sidebar
`flex-grow: 0` on the sidebar
`box-sizing: border-box` on the sidebar
`flex-wrap: nowrap` on the container
questions.why: Flex items default to `flex-shrink: 1`, so when the row overflows every item gives up space in proportion to its size, including the sidebar. `flex-shrink: 0` (or `flex: none`) keeps it at 280px; `flex-grow` only controls growing, and `nowrap` is already the default.
questions.asked: A very common layout bug; the answer shows you know items shrink by default.

questions.q: A `flex-wrap: wrap` container with a fixed height has two rows of items. Which property controls how those rows are spaced within the container?
choices: `align-items`
`justify-content`
`align-content`
`row-gap` only
questions.why: `align-content` distributes the flex lines along the cross axis when there is spare room, while `align-items` aligns items inside each line. `row-gap` sets a fixed gap but does not distribute leftover space.
questions.asked: Separating `align-items` from `align-content` is a common flexbox stumbling block.

questions.q: A designer asks you to show a form's Submit button before the Cancel button on mobile using `order: -1`. What else changes?
choices: Tab order and screen reader order follow the new visual order
Nothing: DOM order, tab order and reading order stay the same
The button is moved in the DOM, so event handlers re-bind
The form will submit with the first button in visual order
questions.why: `order` changes only where the box is painted; keyboard focus and assistive technology follow the DOM. That mismatch can confuse users, so reorder the markup when the new order is meaningful and keep `order` for decorative moves.
questions.asked: Interviewers raise it to see whether you consider keyboard users when you rearrange layouts in CSS.

questions.q: Buttons in a `flex-direction: column` container were full width. After adding `align-items: center` to the container, they shrink to their text width. Why?
choices: `center` also sets `flex: none` on every item
Centring switches the main axis back to horizontal
Items are no longer stretched across the cross axis
Column containers ignore widths once items are centred
questions.why: In a column the cross axis is horizontal, and the full width came from the default `align-items: stretch`. Any other value sizes items to their content, so add `width: 100%` or keep stretch and centre the text instead.
questions.asked: It checks that you can reason about which axis each property controls once the direction changes.

questions.q: The row has plenty of spare space. How wide is `.item`?
choices: 200px, because an explicit `width` beats `flex-basis`
300px, because `flex-basis` beats every other size
250px: basis wins over width, but `max-width` clamps it
275px, the midpoint between the flex basis and the max-width
questions.why: A `flex-basis` other than `auto` replaces `width` as the starting size, so the item wants 300px, but min and max constraints still apply to the result and clamp it to 250px. `width` would only be used if the basis were `auto`.
questions.asked: Knowing the precedence of basis, width and min/max sizes lets you debug flex sizing without trial and error.

questions.q: In a 3-column grid, what does `grid-column: 1 / -1` do to an item?
choices: Spans it from the first to the last explicit column line
Places it in column 1 and hides it on narrow screens
Spans it one column to the left of where it would sit
Places it in the last column, counting backwards
questions.why: Negative line numbers count from the end of the explicit grid, so `-1` is the last line and the item spans every column; that is how full-width headers and error rows are made. It only covers explicit columns, not implicit ones.
questions.asked: A quick placement check; full-width rows inside a grid come up in every dashboard layout.

questions.q: Where does the `<main>` element (with `grid-area: main`) sit in this layout?
choices: First row, beside the header in the 1fr column
Second row, in the 200px column beside the nav
Second row, in the 1fr column beside the nav
Across both columns, below the header row
questions.why: Each quoted string is a row and each name a cell, so `main` is row 2, column 2, which is the `1fr` track. The header spans both columns because its name is repeated in the first row.
questions.asked: Template areas make page layouts readable; interviewers use them to check you can read a grid definition at a glance.

questions.q: A grid has `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)` and `grid-template-rows: 100px 100px`, and holds nine items. How tall is the third row?
choices: 100px, repeating the last explicit row size
0px, since the items fall outside the grid
As tall as its content, via `grid-auto-rows: auto`
Equal to the remaining height of the container
questions.why: Items beyond the explicit grid create implicit tracks, sized by `grid-auto-rows`, whose default is `auto`. Set `grid-auto-rows: 100px` (or `minmax(100px, auto)`) if every row should match.
questions.asked: Explicit versus implicit grid is the concept behind lots of "why is my last row different" bugs.

questions.q: A photo gallery uses `grid-auto-flow: dense`, and wide images now leave no gaps. What is the trade-off?
choices: Items may render out of their DOM order
Every item must declare an explicit row
Wide items are shrunk to fit a single column
The grid can no longer have implicit rows
questions.why: Dense packing backfills earlier holes with later items, so visual order no longer matches source order, which confuses keyboard and screen reader users. It suits galleries where order does not matter and is a poor choice for ordered lists.
questions.asked: It shows you weigh visual polish against reading order.

questions.q: A product grid has three cards per row, with titles of different lengths. You want each card's body and footer to line up with its neighbours. What does that?
choices: Each card spans three rows and uses `grid-template-rows: subgrid`
Give every card `display: flex` and `height: 100%`
Set `align-items: stretch` on the outer product grid
Give each title a fixed `min-height` and `overflow: hidden` on cards
questions.why: With subgrid, each card places its title, body and footer on the parent grid's row tracks, so each row is as tall as the tallest title in it and every section lines up. Flex and stretch only equalise card heights, and fixed heights break on the next long title.
questions.asked: Subgrid is supported everywhere now; knowing when to reach for it shows up-to-date layout skills.

questions.q: What does `gap: 16px 24px` set on a grid container?
choices: 16px between columns and 24px between rows
A gap between 16px and 24px that grows with space
16px inside each cell and 24px around the grid
16px between rows and 24px between columns
questions.why: `gap` is shorthand for `row-gap` then `column-gap`, following the usual block-then-inline order. Gaps only go between tracks, never around the outside edge.
questions.asked: A quick syntax check that trips up people who have only ever written a single value.

questions.q: A 620px-wide grid has `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)` and `gap: 10px`. How wide is each column?
choices: About 206.7px: the gaps are ignored by `fr`
200px: the gaps are taken off before sharing
190px: each column loses 10px on both sides
210px: `fr` shares the gaps between columns
questions.why: Gaps are fixed-size tracks, so `fr` units share what remains: 620 − 2 × 10 = 600px, split three ways. That is why `fr` is safer than percentages, which ignore the gap and overflow.
questions.asked: It checks you know why `repeat(3, 33.33%)` plus a gap overflows, while `fr` does not.

questions.q: What is the shortest way to centre a single child both ways inside a container?
choices: `display: grid; place-items: center;` on the container
`display: block; margin: auto;` on the container
`text-align: center; vertical-align: middle;` on it
`display: flex; align-content: center;` on the container
questions.why: `place-items` sets `align-items` and `justify-items` together, so a one-cell grid centres its child both ways. `margin: auto` on the container centres the container itself, and `align-content` in a single-line flex row does not move the item.
questions.asked: The modern answer to "centre a div"; mention the flex equivalent too.

questions.q: In a 3-column auto-placed grid, items 1 and 2 are normal and item 3 has `grid-column: span 2`. Where does item 3 go?
choices: Row 1, column 3, overflowing into an implicit column
Row 1, column 3, shrunk to fit a single column
Row 2, columns 1–2, leaving row 1, column 3 empty
Row 2, columns 2–3, keeping to its source position
questions.why: A two-column item cannot fit in the single remaining cell, so auto-placement moves to the next row where it fits and, in the default sparse mode, never goes back to fill the hole. `grid-auto-flow: dense` would let a later item fill that cell.
questions.asked: Predicting auto-placement explains the mysterious holes in dashboard grids.

questions.q: A 1000px-wide grid has `gap: 20px`. How many columns does it get?
choices: Four columns of 250px, since 1000 ÷ 250 = 4
Four columns of 235px, shrunk to make room for gaps
Five columns, as `auto-fill` adds an empty one
Three columns of 320px, since four need 1060px
questions.why: `auto-fill` creates as many tracks as fit at their minimum size including the gaps: four would need 4 × 250 + 3 × 20 = 1060px, so it makes three, and `1fr` stretches them to (1000 − 40) ÷ 3 = 320px. Tracks never go below their `minmax()` minimum.
questions.asked: Doing the arithmetic proves you understand the responsive-grid one-liner rather than copying it.

questions.q: A layout uses `grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr`, and a `<pre>` with a very long line in the main column makes the whole page scroll sideways. What is the fix?
choices: Change `1fr` to `minmax(0, 1fr)` for the main column
Change `1fr` to `100%` so it matches the container
Set `overflow: hidden` on the page `<body>`
Change `250px` to `minmax(250px, auto)` for the sidebar
questions.why: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, and the `auto` minimum is the content's min-content width, so an unbreakable line forces the track wider than the space. A minimum of 0 lets the track shrink; then give the `<pre>` `overflow-x: auto`. It is the grid version of the flexbox `min-width: 0` fix.
questions.asked: A deep but very common bug; interviewers are impressed when you know `1fr` has an auto minimum.

questions.q: A badge has `position: relative; top: 10px;`. What happens to the elements around it?
choices: They stay put: its original space is kept
They move down 10px along with the badge
They move up to fill the badge's old space
They overlap it, as it leaves normal flow
questions.why: Relative positioning only shifts where the box is painted; layout still reserves its original position, so nothing else moves. Absolute positioning is what takes an element out of flow.
questions.asked: A basic positioning distinction; mention that `relative` is mostly used to set the containing block for absolute children.

questions.q: Someone puts `z-index: 10` on a plain `<div>` in normal block flow, and it still renders under its neighbour. Why?
choices: z-index needs a value over 100 to beat browser layers
The neighbour comes later in the DOM, which always wins
z-index only applies to positioned, flex or grid items
z-index needs `opacity` below 1 before it takes effect
questions.why: On a statically positioned block, `z-index` is ignored; it takes effect on positioned elements and on flex or grid items. Add `position: relative` (or make the parent flex or grid) and the value will count within its stacking context.
questions.asked: The standard z-index follow-up after stacking contexts; many developers never learned this rule.

questions.q: A sticky header has `z-index: 99999`, yet a `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` appears above it with no z-index at all. Why?
choices: Browsers cap z-index values, so 99999 is ignored
Dialogs get `z-index: 2147483647` from the browser's UA stylesheet
The dialog is rendered in the top layer, above all z-index
Modal dialogs are drawn in a separate OS window
questions.why: Modal dialogs, popovers and fullscreen elements are promoted to the top layer, which paints above the whole document regardless of z-index or stacking contexts. That is why they fix the classic "modal stuck under the header" problem.
questions.asked: It shows you know the platform's built-in answer to z-index wars.

questions.q: Which stylesheet structure is mobile-first?
choices: Desktop styles by default, then `max-width` queries for phones
Only `@media (orientation: portrait)` rules for phone layouts
Two separate stylesheets, chosen by the server from the user-agent string
Narrow styles by default, then `min-width` queries that add to them
questions.why: Mobile-first writes the simplest single-column layout as the base and layers wider layouts on with `min-width` queries, so phones load and override the least CSS. Starting from desktop and undoing it with `max-width` queries is the desktop-first pattern.
questions.asked: A standard responsive-design question; a good answer explains why mobile-first rules are simpler to maintain.

questions.q: A YouTube embed must keep a 16:9 shape at any width. What is the modern CSS?
choices: `height: 56.25vw` on the iframe
`aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%` on it
`object-fit: contain` on the iframe
`padding-top: 16 / 9` on a wrapper
questions.why: `aspect-ratio` sizes one dimension from the other, replacing the old padding-percentage wrapper hack. A `vw` height ties the shape to the viewport rather than the element, and `object-fit` changes how content fits a box, not the box's shape.
questions.asked: Checks you have moved on from legacy embed hacks.

questions.q: User avatars come in all shapes and must fill a 48×48 circle without being squashed. Which declaration on the `` does that?
choices: `object-fit: contain`
`background-size: cover`
`object-fit: cover`
`aspect-ratio: 1`
questions.why: `object-fit: cover` scales the image to fill the box while keeping its proportions, cropping the overflow. `contain` would letterbox it, `background-size` only affects background images, and `aspect-ratio` sets the box shape but still stretches the pixels inside.
questions.asked: An everyday UI detail; mention `object-position` for choosing which part is kept.

questions.q: Cards should lift with a shadow on hover, but on phones the effect sticks after a tap. Which query limits it to devices that can really hover?
choices: `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`
`@media (min-width: 1024px)`
`@media (orientation: landscape)`
`@media (any-pointer: coarse)`
questions.why: Interaction media features describe the input device: `hover: hover` plus `pointer: fine` matches a mouse or trackpad. Width queries misfire on large tablets and small laptops, and `any-pointer: coarse` matches touch devices, the opposite of what you want.
questions.asked: It separates people who use screen width as a proxy for "desktop" from those who query capabilities.

questions.q: Which widths does this query match?
choices: From 400px up to but not including 800px
From 401px up to and including 800px
Nothing: range syntax needs `min-` and `max-`
Only the widths 400px and 800px exactly
questions.why: Media queries level 4 range syntax reads like maths and is supported in all current browsers, so the `<` makes 800px exclusive. The older `min-width`/`max-width` pair is always inclusive, which is why code used `max-width: 799.98px` to avoid overlap.
questions.asked: Checks your CSS is current and that you have met the overlapping-breakpoint problem.

questions.q: Your dark theme sets dark backgrounds with custom properties, but scrollbars, date pickers and checkboxes still render light. What fixes that?
choices: `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root`
`filter: invert(1)` on the form controls
`accent-color: black` on every input
`appearance: none` on the scrollbars
questions.why: `color-scheme` tells the browser which schemes the page supports, so it renders built-in UI such as scrollbars, form controls and the default canvas in the matching scheme. `accent-color` only tints checked controls, and inverting is a hack that breaks images and colours.
questions.asked: Dark mode is a common task; this detail separates a polished implementation from a half-done one.

questions.q: A card component has `@container (min-width: 400px) { .card { display: grid; } }`, but it never switches to grid. No ancestor sets `container-type`. What is wrong?
choices: No ancestor is a query container, so nothing is measured
Container queries only work on direct children of `<body>`
`@container` needs `max-width`; `min-width` is invalid
Container queries need a JavaScript `ResizeObserver` polyfill
questions.why: Container queries test the nearest ancestor that has `container-type` (usually `inline-size`); without one there is nothing to query and the rule never applies. They are supported in all current browsers without JavaScript.
questions.asked: Container queries changed component CSS; interviewers check you know the opt-in step.

questions.q: You put `container-type: inline-size` on `.card` itself and write `@container (min-width: 500px) { .card { display: grid; } }`. Why does the card never change?
choices: An element cannot query its own size, only an ancestor's
`inline-size` containers can only be queried with `max-width`
The rule needs `!important` to beat the card's own `display`
Containers must set an explicit width for queries to work
questions.why: Styles inside `@container` apply to descendants of the query container, because letting an element change its own size based on its size would loop. Put the container on a wrapper, or style the card's children instead.
questions.asked: The most common container-query mistake; explaining the loop shows you understand why the rule exists.

questions.q: A heading inside a card uses `font-size: clamp(1rem, 5cqi, 2rem)`. What is `1cqi`?
choices: 1% of the viewport's inline size, like `vw`
1% of the heading's own inline size
1% of the query container's inline size
1% of the root element's font size
questions.why: Container query units measure the nearest ancestor query container, so text scales with the card rather than the window. If there is no container they fall back to the small viewport units.
questions.asked: It shows you can make components responsive to where they are placed, not just to the screen.

questions.q: No element defines `--accent`. What background does the button get?
choices: Teal, the fallback given as the second argument
Transparent, since the whole declaration is dropped
Black, the initial value for undefined variables
The UA default button background, as if unset
questions.why: The second argument of `var()` is used when the custom property is not defined (its value is the guaranteed-invalid initial value). Fallbacks let components work outside a theme and still pick up tokens when a theme provides them.
questions.asked: The entry question on custom properties; strong answers mention that fallbacks can nest another `var()`.

questions.q: What colour is the paragraph text, if its parent has `color: green`?
questions.code:
p { color: blue; }
p { --c: 20px; color: var(--c); }
choices: Green: the `var()` value is invalid, so `color` inherits
Blue: the invalid declaration is skipped, so the first rule wins
Black: an invalid colour falls back to the initial value
Transparent: the browser cannot parse `20px` as a colour
questions.why: Declarations containing `var()` are accepted at parse time, so this one wins the cascade; when `20px` turns out not to be a colour it is "invalid at computed-value time" and behaves like `unset`, which inherits for `color`. The earlier blue rule has already lost, which surprises people used to invalid CSS simply being skipped.
questions.asked: A deep question about how variables interact with the cascade; it explains why a bad token does not fall back to the previous rule.

questions.q: A team defines `--bp-md: 768px` on `:root` and writes `@media (min-width: var(--bp-md))`. What happens?
choices: It works, because `:root` variables are global
It works only once the page has finished loading
The query is invalid: `var()` cannot be used there
It works in Chromium but not in Firefox or Safari
questions.why: Custom properties belong to elements and are resolved during cascade, while media queries are evaluated for the document without an element, so `var()` is not allowed in them. Teams share breakpoints through a preprocessor, PostCSS custom media, or container queries instead.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand what custom properties actually are, not just that they are "CSS variables".

questions.q: A gradient border rotates via `--angle`, but setting `transition: --angle 1s` just makes it jump. What makes it animate smoothly?
choices: Wrap the angle in `calc()` so it becomes numeric
Use `transition: all 1s` so the property is included
Register it: `@property --angle { syntax: '<angle>'; … }`
Declare `--angle` on `:root` rather than the element
questions.why: An unregistered custom property is just a token list, so the browser cannot interpolate it and swaps it discretely. `@property` gives it a type, an initial value and inheritance, and typed properties can transition and animate.
questions.asked: It shows you know the Houdini-derived `@property` rule and why variables are untyped by default.

questions.q: A progress bar reads `width: var(--progress)`. How do you update the value from JavaScript?
choices: `bar.style.setProperty('--progress', '40%')`
`bar.style.progress = '40%'`
`bar.dataset.progress = '40%'`
`bar.style['var(--progress)'] = '40%'`
questions.why: Custom properties are not exposed as camelCase keys on `style`, so you set them with `setProperty` (and read them with `getPropertyValue`). A `data-` attribute changes the DOM but not any CSS value unless a selector matches it.
questions.asked: Driving CSS from JS through one variable is a clean pattern interviewers like to see.

questions.q: A settings page offers Light, Dark and System themes. Which approach supports all three with the least CSS?
choices: Two stylesheets, swapping the `<link>` element with JavaScript on toggle
A `.dark` class on every component that has colours
Tokens on `:root`, overridden by the OS query and by `data-theme`
A `prefers-color-scheme` query only, as the OS decides
questions.why: Components read colour tokens; the tokens get dark values inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` for `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `[data-theme="dark"]`, so System follows the OS and the attribute forces a choice. A media query alone cannot honour a manual override.
questions.asked: Theming is a common take-home feature; this is the architecture interviewers hope to hear.

questions.q: You write `color: light-dark(#111, #eee)`, yet it always gives `#111`, even with the OS in dark mode. What is missing?
choices: A `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` wrapper
Swapping the order so the dark value comes first
A registered `@property` for the colour value
`color-scheme: light dark` on the element or `:root`
questions.why: `light-dark()` picks a value based on the element's used colour scheme, which is only dark when `color-scheme` allows it and the user prefers it. Without `color-scheme: light dark` the scheme stays light, so the first value always wins.
questions.asked: A modern theming detail; it shows you know how `color-scheme` ties the pieces together.

questions.q: You want a gap twice the size of `--space`. Which declaration works?
choices: `gap: var(--space) * 2;`
`gap: var(--space * 2);`
`gap: calc(var(--space) * 2);`
`gap: 2var(--space);`
questions.why: `var()` substitutes tokens; it does no maths, so arithmetic has to be inside `calc()`. The other forms produce invalid values or invalid `var()` syntax.
questions.asked: A small syntax point that comes up constantly with spacing scales.

questions.q: A component sets `--size: 12` and uses `font-size: var(--size)px`, but the text keeps its inherited size. Why?
choices: Custom properties cannot hold unitless numbers
Substitution keeps tokens separate, so `12` `px` is not a length
Numbers in variables are strings until wrapped in `attr()`
Custom properties must hold a unit of `px` to be usable as a length
questions.why: `var()` substitutes the number token and the following `px` stays a separate identifier, so the result is not the single dimension `12px`. Multiply instead: `calc(var(--size) * 1px)`, which is also how you keep unitless values flexible.
questions.asked: It separates people who understand token substitution from people who treat variables like string templates.

questions.q: Buttons use `--brand` for their background, and a theme can change it. How do you get a slightly darker hover shade without adding another token?
choices: `background: darken(var(--brand), 10%)`
`background: var(--brand); opacity: 0.9`
`background: var(--brand) - 10%`
`background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), black 15%)`
questions.why: `color-mix()` mixes two colours in a chosen colour space at runtime, so it follows whatever `--brand` is. `darken()` is a Sass function that cannot see runtime variables, and `opacity` lets the background through instead of darkening.
questions.asked: Modern colour functions reduce the size of theme token sets; interviewers like seeing you use them.

questions.q: A popover has `transition: opacity 0.3s` and `opacity: 1` when open, and `display: none` plus `opacity: 0` when closed. It still appears instantly. What is missing for the fade-in?
choices: An `@starting-style` block with `opacity: 0` for the open state
A `setTimeout` of 0 between showing it and changing opacity
Changing `display: none` to `visibility: hidden` everywhere
Adding `will-change: opacity` so the browser prepares a layer
questions.why: An element that goes from `display: none` to shown has no previous style to transition from, so it renders at the end state; `@starting-style` supplies that "before" style. The fade-out additionally needs `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` on `display` (and `overlay`) so it is not hidden before the transition runs.
questions.asked: Entry and exit animations used to need JavaScript; knowing `@starting-style` shows your CSS is current.

questions.q: This button fades in its highlight on hover but snaps back instantly when the pointer leaves. Why?
choices: When hover ends, the base rule applies, and it has no transition
Transitions can only run once per element per page load
The `background` shorthand cannot be transitioned in both directions
Leaving an element cancels transitions until the next frame
questions.why: The transition used is the one on the state being entered: on leave, the `.btn` rule applies and has no `transition`, so the change is instant. Put `transition` on the base rule so it covers both directions.
questions.asked: A quick way to see whether someone has written transitions by hand or only copied them.

questions.q: Which pair of properties can the browser usually animate without recalculating layout?
choices: `width` and `height`
`top` and `left`
`transform` and `opacity`
`margin` and `padding`
