questions.why: `transform` and `opacity` change how an already laid-out layer is drawn, so the compositor can animate them without layout or repaint. Animating `left`, `width` or `margin` reruns layout every frame, which is where janky animations come from.
questions.asked: The most common animation question; a strong answer mentions moving with `translate` instead of `left`.

questions.q: A toast slides in with a keyframe animation, then jumps back to its start position when the animation ends. Which property keeps the final frame?
choices: `animation-fill-mode: forwards`
`animation-iteration-count: 1`
`animation-direction: reverse`
`animation-play-state: paused`
questions.why: By default an animation's styles apply only while it runs, so the element falls back to its normal styles afterwards. `forwards` keeps the last keyframe's values; often the cleaner fix is to make the end state the element's normal style.
questions.asked: A small but frequent bug with keyframe animations.

questions.q: An accordion should animate open to its content height. Which approach works in every current browser without JavaScript measurement?
choices: Transition `height` from `0` to `auto`
Transition `max-height` from `0` to `none`
Transition `grid-template-rows` from `0fr` to `1fr`
Transition `transform: scaleY()` from 0 to 1
questions.why: Grid track sizes interpolate, so a one-row grid moving from `0fr` to `1fr` (with `min-height: 0` on the child) animates to the content height. `height: auto` and `max-height: none` are not interpolable without the newer `interpolate-size`, and `scaleY` squashes the content instead of revealing it.
questions.asked: Animating to `auto` is a famous CSS limitation; knowing the grid trick shows practical depth.

questions.q: Some users get motion sickness from your page transitions. How should the CSS respond?
choices: Turn off every animation on screens narrower than 600px, where it matters most
Add an `aria-live` region that announces each transition
Slow every animation down to at least two seconds
Reduce or remove motion in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`
questions.why: The `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature reflects the OS "reduce motion" setting, so you can swap large movements for fades or none at all. Slower animations still move, and screen width says nothing about motion sensitivity.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for it whenever animation comes up; it shows you respect user preferences by default.

questions.q: A card uses `transition: all 0.3s`. What is the main risk?
choices: It stops `transform` from being hardware accelerated
It animates any property that changes, including layout ones
It overrides every transition declared on child elements as well
It is deprecated and ignored in current browsers
questions.why: `all` animates whatever happens to change, such as `width`, `padding` or colours from a theme switch, causing unexpected motion and layout work. Listing the properties you mean (`transform`, `opacity`, `background-color`) keeps behaviour predictable.
questions.asked: A code-review question; it shows you think about side effects in CSS the way you would in code.

questions.q: A skeleton loader has `animation: shimmer 2s infinite` and `animation-delay: -0.5s`. What does the negative delay do?
choices: Waits 0.5s before starting, like a positive delay
Plays the animation backwards for the first 0.5s
Is invalid, so the animation starts with no delay
Starts at once, as if it had already run for 0.5s
questions.why: A negative delay starts the animation immediately part-way through its cycle. Giving each skeleton row a different negative delay staggers them without any waiting at the start.
questions.asked: A neat trick that shows you have built loading states and know the animation properties beyond the shorthand.

questions.q: A loading spinner rotates with `animation: spin 1s infinite`, and it visibly speeds up and slows down each turn. What is the fix?
choices: Set the timing function to `linear`
Set `animation-direction: alternate`
Set `animation-fill-mode: both`
Set `animation-duration` below 500ms
questions.why: The default timing function is `ease`, which accelerates and decelerates within every iteration. `linear` gives a constant rotation speed, which is what a spinner needs; `alternate` would make it spin back and forth.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know the default easing and how it affects repeated animations.

questions.q: An old page has no `<!DOCTYPE html>` line. What is the practical effect?
choices: The browser refuses to run any JavaScript on the page
The page is parsed as XML instead, and fails on the first markup error
The browser renders it in quirks mode with legacy CSS rules
Nothing: the doctype has been optional since HTML5
questions.why: Without the doctype, browsers switch to quirks mode, which emulates old engines: for example, percentage heights and table font sizes behave differently. The short HTML5 doctype exists only to trigger standards mode.
questions.asked: It explains layout bugs that only happen in some legacy pages or HTML emails.

questions.q: A template renders `<button disabled="false">Save</button>`. Is the button disabled?
choices: No: the string "false" turns the attribute off
Only in Safari, which parses the value as a string
No: boolean attributes only work without a value
Yes: any presence of a boolean attribute means true
questions.why: For boolean attributes like `disabled`, `checked` and `required`, the attribute being present means true, whatever its value. To enable the button, remove the attribute (or set the `disabled` property to `false` from JavaScript).
questions.asked: A common bug when templates render attributes from variables; frameworks hide it, which is why interviewers ask it.

choices:
A `

A `
` wrapped by a `

` with the text split in two
An error page, since the markup is invalid

questions.why:
A `

questions.asked: It explains confusing hydration and styling bugs, and shows you know HTML is error-correcting rather than strict.

questions.q: A form shows the account id in a field users must not change. Which attribute still sends the value when the form is submitted?
choices: `disabled`, which also stops the user editing it
`readonly`, which blocks editing but still submits
`inert`, which blocks editing and keeps it in the form
`aria-disabled`, which disables the native input
questions.why: Disabled controls are left out of the form data set entirely, while `readonly` fields cannot be edited but are submitted. `inert` stops interaction but does not affect submission, and `aria-disabled` only informs assistive technology.
questions.asked: A common "why is this field missing on the server" bug.

questions.q: A shipping address section should be disabled until "Ship to a different address" is ticked. What is the simplest markup?
choices: Wrap the fields in `<fieldset disabled>` and toggle that
Add `disabled` to each input and toggle them one by one
Set `pointer-events: none` on the section container
Wrap them in `<div aria-disabled="true">` and toggle it
questions.why: A disabled `<fieldset>` disables every control inside it (except in its first `<legend>`), so one attribute switches the section and the fields are also left out of the submission. `pointer-events` still allows keyboard input, and `aria-disabled` changes nothing functionally.
questions.asked: It shows you reach for native grouping rather than looping over inputs in JavaScript.

questions.q: A layout puts the Notes `<textarea>` in a sidebar, outside the `<form id="checkout">` element. How can it still be submitted with the form?
choices: Give it `name="checkout"` so it joins that form
Wrap it in a second form with the same `action`
It cannot; only descendants of a form element are ever submitted
Give it `form="checkout"`, which links it by the form's id
questions.why: The `form` attribute associates a control with any form by id, wherever it sits in the document, and it is included in submission and `FormData`. `name` is the field's key in the payload, not a link to a form.
questions.asked: Handy when layout and form structure disagree; many developers do not know the attribute exists.

questions.q: A postcode field has `pattern="[0-9]{5}"`. Is the value `123456` valid?
choices: Yes, because the first five characters match
Yes, because patterns match anywhere in the value
No, because the pattern must match the whole value
No, because `pattern` needs `^` and `$` to work at all
questions.why: The browser wraps `pattern` as `^(?:…)$`, so the entire value must match, and six digits fail. Adding your own anchors is harmless but unnecessary; the empty value is only rejected if the field is also `required`.
questions.asked: A small constraint-validation detail that trips people who copy JavaScript regexes into HTML.

questions.q: Required fields show a red border as soon as the page loads, before the user has typed anything. Which selector should the styles use instead of `:invalid`?
choices: `:user-invalid`
`:invalid:focus`
`:not(:valid)`
`:placeholder-shown`
questions.why: `:user-invalid` only matches after the user has interacted with the field or tried to submit, so an empty required field is not flagged on load. `:invalid` matches immediately, `:not(:valid)` is the same thing, and styling only on focus hides errors once the user moves on.
questions.asked: Premature error styling is a common UX complaint; this is the native fix interviewers hope you know.

questions.q: A form has Publish and Save draft buttons. Drafts may be incomplete. How do you skip browser validation for Save draft only?
choices: Add `novalidate` to the `<form>` element
Add `formnovalidate` to the Save draft button
Make Save draft `type="button"` and call `form.submit()`
Remove `required` in the draft button's click handler
questions.why: `formnovalidate` on a submit button turns validation off only for submissions made with that button, while Publish still validates. `novalidate` on the form turns it off for both, and removing `required` in a handler is fragile and leaves the form changed.
questions.asked: It shows you know the per-button form attributes (`formaction`, `formmethod`, `formnovalidate`).

questions.q: A price field is `<input type="number" min="0">`, and the browser rejects 9.99 as invalid. Why?
choices: The default `step` is 1, so 9.99 is not a valid step
Number inputs only accept integers in every browser
`min="0"` forces whole numbers when it is present
Decimals need `inputmode="decimal"` to be accepted
questions.why: Number inputs validate against `step`, which defaults to 1 counted from `min`, so 9.99 is a step mismatch. Set `step="0.01"` (or `step="any"`); `inputmode` only changes the on-screen keyboard.
questions.asked: A real bug in checkout forms; knowing `step` shows you have shipped number fields.

questions.q: A confirmation `<dialog>` contains `<form method="dialog">` with OK and Cancel buttons that have `value` attributes. What happens when OK is clicked?
choices: The page posts the form to its own URL and reloads
Nothing, until a click handler calls `dialog.close()`
The dialog closes and `returnValue` is set to OK's value
The dialog closes, and the values go to its `action` URL
questions.why: A form with `method="dialog"` does not send a request: submitting it closes the enclosing dialog and sets `dialog.returnValue` to the submitter's value, and a `close` event fires. It is a no-JavaScript way to build a confirm dialog.
questions.asked: It shows you know the native dialog features beyond `showModal()`.

questions.q: What does this markup give you without any JavaScript?
choices: A modal dialog that traps focus until closed
A tooltip that opens on hover and on focus
A menu that is always visible on wide screens
A toggling top-layer panel that closes on Esc or outside click
questions.why: The popover attribute gives a top-layer element that the button toggles; the default `auto` popovers light-dismiss on Escape or an outside click. It is not modal and does not trap focus, which is what `<dialog>` with `showModal()` is for.
questions.asked: Popovers replace a lot of dropdown JavaScript; interviewers use this to see if your platform knowledge is current.

questions.q:
A JSX habit leaks into a server template: `

Hello

`. What does the HTML parser do?
choices: Creates an empty div, then the paragraph after it
Reports a syntax error in the console and stops rendering the page
Drops the div, since self-closing divs are invalid
Ignores the slash, so the paragraph ends up inside the div
questions.why:
In HTML the trailing slash is ignored; it only means something on void elements like ``, where it is optional anyway. The `
` stays open and swallows the following content until something closes it.
questions.asked: It separates people who know HTML from people who only know JSX, where `<div />` is valid.

questions.q:
A table is written as `
…
`. Why does the CSS rule `table > tr { … }` match nothing?
choices: The parser inserts a `<tbody>`, so rows are not direct children
Rows can only be styled through their `<td>` cells
The child combinator does not work on table elements
`table > tr` needs `display: table-row` set on the rows before it matches
questions.why: When a `<tr>` appears directly in a `<table>`, the HTML parser wraps it in an implied `<tbody>`, so the real structure is `table > tbody > tr`. Write `tbody > tr` or `table tr` instead.
questions.asked: A parsing detail that explains otherwise baffling selector and DOM-traversal bugs.

questions.q: A required-field marker uses `.required::after { color: red; }`, but no asterisk ever appears. What is missing?
choices: A `content: "*"` declaration, without which no box is made
`display: block`, since pseudo-elements start out hidden
A `position` value, as pseudo-elements need positioning
An `aria-hidden` attribute on the element being marked
questions.why: `::before` and `::after` only generate a box when `content` is set to something other than `none`, even an empty string. Everything else about the pseudo-element is optional.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have built decorations with pseudo-elements rather than extra markup.

questions.q: Which selector adds a download icon only to links that point at PDF files?
choices: `a[href*="pdf"]`
`a[href$=".pdf"]`
`a[href^=".pdf"]`
`a[type="pdf"]`
questions.why: `$=` matches attribute values that end with the string, `^=` matches the start and `*=` matches anywhere, so `*="pdf"` would also catch `/pdf-guide.html`. The `type` attribute is optional and rarely set on links.
questions.asked: Attribute selectors come up when styling generated content you cannot add classes to.

questions.q: A product carousel scrolls sideways, and each card should settle neatly at the left edge after a swipe. Which CSS does that?
choices: `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` on the track, `scroll-snap-align: start` on cards
`overflow-x: auto; scroll-behavior: smooth` on the track
`scroll-padding: 0` on the track and `scroll-margin: 0` on each card
`overscroll-behavior-x: contain` on the track and `display: flex` on it
questions.why: Scroll snapping needs both halves: the container opts in with `scroll-snap-type`, and each child declares where it snaps with `scroll-snap-align`. `scroll-behavior` only smooths programmatic scrolls, and `overscroll-behavior` controls scroll chaining.
questions.asked: Carousels are common UI; this shows you know the no-JavaScript approach.

questions.q: You want a subgrid layout where supported and a flexbox fallback elsewhere. Which rule applies styles only when the browser understands a declaration?
choices: `@media (feature: subgrid) { … }`
`@layer supports.subgrid { … }`
`@container style(subgrid) { … }`
`@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) { … }`
questions.why: `@supports` tests whether the browser can parse a property and value, so you can layer enhancements on a working base. Media queries describe the device, not CSS support.
questions.asked: Feature queries are the CSS side of progressive enhancement, which interviewers like to hear about.

questions.q: What does `width: min(100%, 60rem)` do on a page's content column?
choices: Keeps it at least 60rem wide, even on phones
Fills the parent up to a cap of 60rem
Always sets it to exactly 60rem wide
Sets it to 60% of the root font size
questions.why: `min()` picks the smaller value, so on narrow screens the column is 100% of its parent and on wide screens it stops at 60rem. It replaces the `width: 100%; max-width: 60rem` pair in one declaration.
questions.asked: CSS maths functions reduce media queries; interviewers like the one-line version.

questions.q: A signup form has `<input type="checkbox" name="newsletter">` with no `value` attribute. What is submitted when it is ticked, and when it is not?
choices: `newsletter=true` when ticked; `newsletter=false` when not
`newsletter=1` when ticked; `newsletter=0` when not
`newsletter=on` when ticked; nothing at all when not
`newsletter=` when ticked; `newsletter=off` when not
questions.why: A checked checkbox sends its `value`, which defaults to `"on"`, and an unchecked one is omitted from the form data entirely. Server code must treat a missing key as false.
questions.asked: It causes real bugs in server handlers that expect an explicit false value.

questions.q: A city field should suggest common cities but still accept any text the user types. Which native element fits?
choices: An `<input list="cities">` with a `<datalist>`
A `<select>` whose first option is empty
An `<input type="search">` with `pattern`
An `<output>` element bound to the input
questions.why: A `<datalist>` attached with the `list` attribute offers suggestions while leaving the field free text. A `<select>` restricts the value to its options, and `<output>` displays results rather than taking input.
questions.asked: Knowing the native option can save a dependency in simple cases.

questions.q: A logo is always shown at 120×40 CSS pixels. How should the `` offer a sharper version for high-density screens?
choices: `srcset="logo.png 120w, logo@2x.png 240w"` without `sizes`
A `<picture>` with one `<source media>` per pixel ratio
Only `logo@2x.png` with CSS `zoom: 0.5` applied to it
`srcset="logo.png 1x, logo@2x.png 2x"` with `src="logo.png"`
questions.why: For a fixed-size image, `x` descriptors let the browser pick by device pixel ratio. `w` descriptors are for images whose layout width varies, and without `sizes` the browser assumes the image is `100vw` wide and may download far too much.
questions.asked: It checks you know when to use `x` versus `w` descriptors.

questions.q: A React component imports `styles from './Card.module.css'` and uses `className={styles.title}`. What happens to the `.title` class?
choices: It stays `.title` and applies to every `.title` on the page
It is inlined as a `style` attribute on the element
It is renamed to a unique class scoped to this module
It is moved into the component's shadow root
questions.why: CSS Modules rewrite each class to a unique name at build time (for example `Card_title__a1b2`) and export the mapping, so styles cannot collide across components. Global styles need an explicit `:global()` escape.
questions.asked: Teams ask how you scope CSS in a component app; CSS Modules is one of the standard answers.

questions.q: In BEM naming, what does the class `card__title--muted` describe?
choices: The `muted` element inside the `title` block
The `title` element of `card`, in its `muted` variant
A `card` block nested inside a `title` block
A utility class that mutes any card title text
questions.why: BEM is Block__Element--Modifier: `card` is the block, `title` an element of it, and `muted` a variant. The flat, single-class selectors keep specificity low and predictable.
questions.asked: Naming conventions come up in CSS architecture questions; explain why BEM keeps specificity flat.

questions.q: On short pages the footer floats halfway up the screen. The layout is `<body>` → `<header>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`. What keeps the footer at the bottom?
choices: `position: fixed; bottom: 0` on the footer, with no other change
`margin-top: 100vh` on the footer so it starts below the fold
A `min-height: 100dvh` flex column on `body`, with `main { flex: 1 }`
`height: 100%` on `<main>` so it fills the rest of the page
questions.why: Making the body at least viewport-tall and letting `main` grow pushes the footer down on short pages while still letting long pages scroll normally. A fixed footer covers content on long pages, and `height: 100%` on `main` has nothing definite to resolve against.
questions.asked: The "sticky footer" is a classic layout task; the flex version shows you think in terms of free space.

questions.q: A table hides filtered rows with the `hidden` attribute, and the zebra stripes break. Which selector stripes only the visible rows?
choices: `tr:nth-child(even of :not([hidden]))`
`tr:not([hidden]):nth-child(even)`
`tr:nth-of-type(even):not([hidden])`
`tr:visible:nth-child(even)`
questions.why: The `of S` form of `:nth-child()` counts only siblings matching S, so the even count skips hidden rows. The other forms still count hidden rows, and `:visible` is a jQuery pseudo-class, not CSS.
questions.asked: It shows you know selector features added in the last few years, not just CSS2.

questions.q: A heading and its subheading have different font sizes. Why do the subheading's lines overlap when the parent has `line-height: 1.2em`, but not with `line-height: 1.2`?
choices: `em` line heights ignore the font size of children entirely
A unitless value is always rounded up to a whole pixel
The `em` value is computed on the parent, and children inherit those pixels
`1.2` is treated as 1.2rem, which is based on the root size
questions.why: A length like `1.2em` is resolved to pixels on the parent and that fixed value is inherited, so larger child text gets a line box that is too short. A unitless number is inherited as a factor and recalculated against each element's own font size.
questions.asked: The reason style guides say "always use unitless line-height"; interviewers want the inheritance explanation.

questions.q: Clicking an in-page link like `#pricing` scrolls the heading under your 64px sticky header. What fixes it in CSS?
choices: `scroll-margin-top: 64px` on each target (or `scroll-padding-top`)
`margin-top: -64px` on the sticky header element
`scroll-behavior: smooth` on the `<html>` element
`position: relative; top: 64px` on each target heading
questions.why: `scroll-margin` on the target (or `scroll-padding` on the scroll container) offsets where the browser stops when it scrolls something into view, including for anchors and `scrollIntoView`. Smooth scrolling changes the animation, not the final position.
questions.asked: Every site with a sticky header meets this; the CSS-only fix is what interviewers want.

questions.q: When a filter reduces a list so it no longer overflows, the scrollbar disappears and the whole layout shifts sideways. Which property prevents that shift?
choices: `overflow-y: scroll`, which hides the scrollbar when unused
`scrollbar-width: none`, which keeps the gutter in place
`overscroll-behavior: contain` on the list container
`scrollbar-gutter: stable` on the scrolling container
questions.why: `scrollbar-gutter: stable` reserves space for the scrollbar whether or not content overflows, so the content width stays the same. `overflow-y: scroll` also avoids the shift, but by always showing an empty scrollbar, and `scrollbar-width: none` hides the scrollbar entirely.
questions.asked: A polish detail that shows you notice layout shift in real UIs.

questions.q: A modal's content scrolls, and when the user reaches its end the page behind starts scrolling too. Which property stops that?
choices: `overflow: hidden` on the modal's scroll area
`touch-action: none` on the whole `<body>` element
`scroll-snap-stop: always` on the modal's children
`overscroll-behavior: contain` on the modal's scroll area
questions.why: `overscroll-behavior: contain` stops scroll chaining, so reaching the edge of the modal does not hand the scroll to its ancestors. `overflow: hidden` would stop the modal scrolling at all, and `touch-action: none` breaks touch scrolling everywhere.
questions.asked: It is a small property that replaces a lot of scroll-lock JavaScript.

questions.q: A form has `<select name="country"><option>France</option><option>Spain</option></select>`, and the user picks Spain. What is submitted?
choices: `country=1`, the index of the chosen option
`country=Spain`, the option's text content
`country=`, since no `value` attributes exist
`country=on`, as for a checkbox with no value
questions.why: When an `<option>` has no `value` attribute, its value is its text content. Relying on that couples your API to display text, so real forms set explicit values such as ISO codes.
questions.asked: It shows you know what the browser actually sends rather than what the UI displays.

questions.q: An `` has `srcset="a-400.jpg 400w, a-800.jpg 800w, a-1600.jpg 1600w"` but no `sizes`, and it is shown in a 300px sidebar on a 1440px laptop. What happens?
choices: The browser assumes `100vw` and downloads a far larger file
The browser measures the sidebar and picks the 400w file
The `srcset` is ignored and `src` is used, as `sizes` is required
The browser always picks the smallest candidate to save data
questions.why: The browser chooses a candidate before layout, so without `sizes` it assumes the image will be as wide as the viewport and picks something suitable for 1440px or more. Setting `sizes` (for example `300px`) tells it the real slot width.
questions.asked: The most common responsive-image mistake; the answer shows you know why `sizes` exists.

questions.q: The hero shows a wide landscape photo on desktop but should switch to a tightly cropped portrait photo on phones. Which markup expresses that?
choices: A `` with `` per crop and an `` fallback
One `` whose `srcset` lists both crops with `w` descriptors
Two `` elements, one hidden by a media query at each size
One `` with `object-position` set for each breakpoint
questions.why: Art direction, where different images are needed, is what `` with `media` conditions is for; the browser must use the source that matches. `srcset` alone treats candidates as the same image at different resolutions and may pick either, and hidden `` elements can still download.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see if you know the difference between resolution switching and art direction.

questions.q: In which order should these go inside `<picture>` so browsers get the best format they support?
choices: Any order: the browser compares all sources by file size
JPEG first, so older browsers can stop there quickly
As shown: the first `<source>` it supports is used
WebP first, as it is supported more widely than AVIF
questions.why: The browser walks the `` elements in order and uses the first whose `type` (and `media`) it supports, falling back to the ``. Putting the most efficient format first means capable browsers get it; `alt` and sizing live on the `` either way.
questions.asked: A practical question about serving modern formats with a safe fallback.

questions.q: Inside a web component's shadow CSS, which selector styles the custom element itself, for example to give it `display: block`?
choices: `:root`
`:scope > *`
`::part(host)`
`:host`
questions.why: `:host` selects the shadow host from inside its shadow tree, and `:host(.compact)` matches it with a class. Custom elements are `display: inline` by default, so most components set `:host { display: block; }`.
questions.asked: The first thing anyone writes when styling a component; it shows hands-on web component experience.

questions.q: The page stylesheet has `.btn { background: purple; }`, but buttons inside a component's shadow root stay grey. What does reach inside the shadow tree?
choices: Nothing at all: shadow trees ignore all outside CSS
Only rules that use `!important` from the page
Custom properties and other inherited properties
Page rules whose selectors include the element name
questions.why: Shadow DOM scopes selectors, so page rules cannot match elements inside it, but inheritance still flows from the host into the tree. That is why design tokens are passed in as custom properties such as `--button-bg`.
questions.asked: It shows you understand how theming works across the shadow boundary.

questions.q: A `<date-picker>` component's docs say it exposes `part="header"`. How do you style that header from the page?
choices: `date-picker .header { … }`
`date-picker::part(header) { … }`
`date-picker >>> header { … }`
`date-picker::slotted(header) { … }`
questions.why: Elements marked with `part` inside a shadow root are styleable from outside with `::part()`, which is the component's explicit styling API. Descendant selectors cannot cross the boundary, `>>>` was removed years ago, and `::slotted` is used inside the component.
questions.asked: It shows you can theme third-party web components without forking them.

questions.q:
A component's shadow CSS has `::slotted(p) strong { color: red; }` and `::slotted(p) { margin: 0; }`. What applies to `

Hi there

` slotted in from the page?
choices: Both: `::slotted` reaches any slotted descendant
Neither: slotted content only takes page styles
Only the colour, as margins cannot cross the boundary
Only the margin: `::slotted` cannot reach descendants
questions.why: `::slotted()` takes a single compound selector and matches only the top-level nodes placed in a slot, so `::slotted(p) strong` is invalid. The slotted content stays in the light DOM, so the page can style its inner parts itself.
questions.asked: A deep web component detail; the answer shows you know slotted content lives in the light DOM.

questions.q: The page sets `body { color: navy; font-family: Inter; }`. What does text inside a component's shadow root use, if its own CSS sets neither?
choices: Navy and Inter, because inherited properties cross the shadow boundary
The browser defaults, as shadow roots start from a fresh stylesheet
Navy but not Inter, since fonts must be declared inside the shadow
Inter but not navy, since colours are reset at every shadow host
questions.why: Encapsulation blocks selectors, not inheritance: the shadow tree inherits from its host like any child. A component that must be immune can reset with `:host { all: initial; }`, at the cost of losing theming.
questions.asked: A common misconception about shadow DOM; getting it right shows you understand what encapsulation actually covers.

questions.q: A component's shadow CSS has `:host { display: block; }`, and the page has `user-card { display: inline-flex; }`. What display does the element get?
choices: `inline-flex`: outer styles beat `:host` rules
`block`: the component's own styles always win
`block`: `:host` has higher specificity than a tag
`inline-flex`: the page stylesheet loads later
questions.why: For normal declarations, styles from the outer context win over `:host` rules regardless of specificity or order, so `:host` acts as a default the page can override. The order flips for `!important`, letting a component lock a value.
questions.asked: It shows you understand the cascade across shadow boundaries, not just inside one tree.

questions.q: A component builds classes like `` `text-${color}-600` `` with Tailwind, and the colours only work for some values. Why?
choices: Tailwind limits each component to a fixed set of colours
Template literals are not allowed in `className` in React
The build scans source for whole class names, so these are never generated
Classes are generated at runtime, which is too late for first paint
questions.why: Tailwind generates only classes it finds as complete strings in your source, so dynamically assembled names are missing unless they appear elsewhere, which is why "some" work. Map values to full class names (`{ red: 'text-red-600' }`) or safelist them.
questions.asked: A common Tailwind bug; the answer shows you understand how its build step works.

questions.q: An element has `style="color: red"`, and a stylesheet has `p { color: blue !important; }`. What colour is it?
choices: Red: inline styles always beat any stylesheet
Blue: element selectors outrank the `style` attribute
Red: inline styles count as `!important` as well
Blue: an important declaration beats a normal inline one
questions.why: Importance is compared before specificity, so an `!important` stylesheet rule beats a normal inline style; only an inline `!important` would beat it back. Inline styles win otherwise because they have the highest specificity, not because they are special.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you know importance and specificity are separate steps.

questions.q: A two-column flex layout has a filter sidebar with `position: sticky; top: 0`. It scrolls away with the page instead of sticking. No ancestor has `overflow` set. What is the likely cause?
choices: Sticky elements cannot be flex items in any browser
The sidebar is stretched to the row's full height, so it has no room to move
The `top` value must be larger than zero for sticking to start
Flex containers create a new stacking context that stops sticking
questions.why: A sticky element only moves within its containing block, and the default `align-items: stretch` makes the sidebar as tall as the row, so there is no space to stick into. `align-self: start` on the sidebar keeps it content-height so it can stick.
questions.asked: A subtle and common sticky bug; explaining the containing-block rule shows real understanding.

questions.q: To stop a carousel spilling sideways, you add `overflow-x: hidden` to its wrapper. Now a dropdown inside it is clipped vertically, and the wrapper has a vertical scrollbar. Why?
choices: `visible` cannot pair with `hidden`, so `overflow-y` becomes `auto`
Hidden overflow on one axis always hides the other axis too
Dropdowns are clipped by any ancestor with a set `overflow`
Horizontal clipping creates a stacking context that clips it
questions.why: If one axis is `hidden`, `scroll` or `auto`, a `visible` value on the other axis computes to `auto`, turning the wrapper into a scroll container. `overflow-x: clip` clips without creating a scroll container, so `overflow-y` can stay visible.
questions.asked: It explains a whole class of "where did this scrollbar come from" bugs and shows you know `clip`.

questions.q: A decorative child has `position: absolute; z-index: -1` to sit behind its card's text, but it disappears behind the card's white background. What fixes it?
choices: Give the child `z-index: 0` so it sits at the card's level
Give the card `overflow: hidden` to contain the child
Move the child after the text so it paints first
Give the card `isolation: isolate` so it forms a stacking context
questions.why: Without a stacking context on the card, the child's negative z-index places it behind the card's own background within the parent stacking context. Making the card a stacking context keeps the child above the card's background but below its in-flow text.
questions.asked: Knowing the painting order within a stacking context is what separates deep CSS knowledge from trial and error.

questions.q: With native CSS nesting, what is the specificity of the inner rule when it matches an element through `.a`?
choices: (0,2,0), from `.a .c`, since only `.a` matched
(1,1,0), because it behaves like `:is(.a, #b) .c`
(0,1,0), because the parent adds no specificity
(1,2,0), as all selectors in the list are summed
questions.why: Nested rules desugar the parent list into `:is()`, which takes the specificity of its most specific argument, so `#b` gives the rule id weight even when `.a` is what matched. Sass expands to `.a .c, #b .c` instead, so migrating from Sass can change which rule wins.
questions.asked: A deep difference between native nesting and Sass that bites teams during migration.

questions.q: The viewport is 1200px wide at a pixel ratio of 1. Which slot width does the browser use to pick from `srcset`?
choices: 600px, from the first condition that matches
396px, from the most specific matching condition
1200px, from the final `100vw` default value
400px, the smallest candidate in the `srcset`
questions.why: The browser uses the first entry in `sizes` whose media condition matches, and `(min-width: 600px)` already matches at 1200px, so the slot is 50vw = 600px and it will pick the 800w file. List conditions from widest to narrowest so the later ones are ever reached.
questions.asked: Reading a `sizes` attribute correctly is how you catch images that download the wrong file at some breakpoints.
